drills.los_text: discuss the objectives and scope of the GIPS standards and their benefits to prospective clients and investors, as well as investment managers
drills.reading_name: Overview of the Global Investment Performance Standards

questions.stem: The mission of the GIPS standards is most likely to:

options.A: guarantee the accuracy of every portfolio return a compliant firm reports.
options.B: promote ethics and integrity and instill trust through use of the standards.
options.C: establish a mandatory regime enforced by national securities regulators.

rationales.A: The GIPS standards govern the calculation and presentation of composite-level performance so that reported results are accurate and comparable; they do not certify or guarantee each portfolio-level number a firm reports to an individual client. The mission is framed in terms of ethics, integrity and trust, not of guaranteeing individual returns.
rationales.B: The mission of the GIPS standards is to promote ethics and integrity and instill trust through the use of the GIPS standards by achieving universal demand for compliance by asset owners, adoption by asset managers, and support from regulators for the ultimate benefit of the global investment community. Each element matters: demand comes from asset owners, adoption from asset managers, and support, rather than enforcement, from regulators.
rationales.C: GIPS compliance is voluntary and ethics-driven. The mission seeks universal demand for compliance by asset owners, adoption by asset managers and support from regulators, not a mandatory regulatory regime enforced by national securities regulators. A compliant firm must still follow all applicable laws and regulations, but the standards themselves are self-regulatory rather than statutory.

questions.stem: An objective of the GIPS standards is most likely to:

options.A: guarantee that compliant firms produce uniform investment returns.
options.B: promote government regulation of performance reporting in each market.
options.C: promote investor interests and instill investor confidence.

rationales.A: The GIPS standards standardize the calculation and presentation of performance so that reported results are accurate and comparable; they do not, and cannot, guarantee uniform investment returns across compliant firms. Comparability of reporting is not uniformity of results, and two firms following the standards faithfully will still report very different performance.
rationales.B: One of the five objectives is to promote industry self-regulation on a global basis, which is the opposite of promoting government regulation of performance reporting in each national market. A compliant firm must still adhere to all applicable laws and regulations, but the standards themselves are voluntary and self-regulatory in character.
rationales.C: The five objectives of the GIPS standards are to: promote investor interests and instill investor confidence; ensure accurate and consistent data; obtain worldwide acceptance of a single standard for calculating and presenting performance; promote fair, global competition among investment firms; and promote industry self-regulation on a global basis.

questions.stem: A claim of compliance with the GIPS Standards for Firms is most likely available to:

options.A: firms whose discretionary assets exceed a minimum size threshold.
options.B: discretionary managers and asset owners that compete for business.
options.C: any financial services organization, including custodians and consultants.

rationales.A: No asset-size threshold exists for claiming compliance, so a cut-off such as $1 billion in discretionary assets is invented. Eligibility turns on what the entity is and how it is held out to the market, namely a firm or asset owner that manages assets on a discretionary basis and competes for business, not on assets under management. Compliance must, however, be achieved on a firm-wide basis rather than for selected products.
rationales.B: Only investment management firms and asset owners that manage assets on a discretionary basis, and that compete for business, may claim compliance with the GIPS Standards for Firms. An asset owner that manages investments directly and/or through the use of external managers on behalf of participants, beneficiaries, or the organization itself, but does not compete for business, would instead comply with the GIPS Standards for Asset Owners. Consultants, software houses, and third-party performance measurement providers such as custodians may not claim to be GIPS-compliant. GIPS compliance cannot be claimed for only some of a firm's products, nor for specific composites, pooled funds, or portfolios; compliance can be achieved only on a firm-wide basis.
rationales.C: Consultants, software houses, and third-party performance measurement providers such as custodians may not claim to be GIPS-compliant. The claim is available only to investment management firms and asset owners that manage assets on a discretionary basis and compete for business; an asset owner that does not compete for business complies instead with the GIPS Standards for Asset Owners.

questions.stem: An unscrupulous practice that the GIPS standards are designed to prevent is most likely to:

options.A: charge performance-based fees without obtaining client consent.
options.B: present returns for only the best-performing portfolios.
options.C: trade ahead of client orders to boost reported firm returns.

rationales.A: Fee arrangements are a contractual matter between a firm and its clients, and a performance-based fee disclosed to and agreed with a client is not a performance-presentation abuse at all. The GIPS standards target misrepresentation in the calculation and presentation of performance, such as showing only the best-performing portfolios as though they represented the firm's expertise in a given strategy.
rationales.B: Unscrupulous employees might attempt to gather and retain assets by misrepresenting a firm's historical record: presenting returns only for the best-performing portfolios as though those returns fully represented the firm's expertise in a given strategy or style; basing portfolio values on their own unsubstantiated estimates of asset prices; inflating returns by annualizing partial-period results; selecting the most favorable measurement period, calculating returns from a low point to a high point; presenting simulated returns as though they had actually been earned; choosing as a benchmark the particular index the selected portfolios have outperformed by the greatest margin during the preferred measurement period; portraying the growth of assets in the style or strategy of interest so as to mask the difference between investment returns and client contributions; or using the marketing department's expertise in graphic design to underplay unfavorable performance data and direct the prospect's attention to the most persuasive elements of the sales presentation. Cherry-picking the best portfolios is the classic abuse composite construction is built to prevent.
rationales.C: Front-running is a trading and ethics violation addressed by the Code and Standards, not a performance-presentation abuse. The GIPS standards target misleading calculation and presentation practices: cherry-picking top portfolios, annualizing partial-period results, selecting a favorable measurement window, presenting simulated returns as though actually earned, and similar misrepresentations of the historical record.

questions.stem: Under the GIPS Standards for Firms, a person who has expressed interest in, and qualifies to invest through, a segregated account managed to one of the firm's strategies is most likely referred to as a:

options.A: prospective client.
options.B: prospective investor.
options.C: prospective client or prospective investor, used interchangeably.

rationales.A: A prospective client is any person or entity that has expressed interest in one of the firm's strategies and qualifies to invest in that strategy via a segregated account, irrespective of whether the person or entity currently invests with the firm through another strategy that the firm offers. A prospective investor, by contrast, is any person or entity that has expressed interest in one of the firm's pooled funds and qualifies to invest in that pooled fund, again irrespective of any other current investments with the firm. The person described here is interested in a segregated account, so the term that applies is prospective client.
rationales.B: Prospective investor is the pooled fund term. A person interested in a segregated account managed to one of the firm's strategies is a prospective client; a prospective investor is one who has expressed interest in, and qualifies to invest in, one of the firm's pooled funds. The distinction drives different delivery obligations, with GIPS Reports going to prospective clients and GIPS Pooled Fund Reports to prospective pooled fund investors.
rationales.C: The two terms are distinct rather than interchangeable: one attaches to segregated-account strategies and the other to pooled funds, and each additionally requires that the person or entity qualify to invest in the strategy or fund concerned. Simply requesting marketing material does not make someone either a prospective client or a prospective investor.

questions.stem: A benefit of GIPS compliance to an investment management firm is most likely:

options.A: a guarantee of winning the institutional mandates it competes for.
options.B: an exemption from local performance-advertising laws.
options.C: the removal of a serious competitive impediment in manager searches.

rationales.A: Compliance removes a serious competitive impediment and is routinely screened for in requests for proposals, but it does not guarantee that the firm wins any particular mandate. In many markets it is a necessary credential rather than a sufficient one.
rationales.B: A compliant firm must comply with all applicable laws and regulations governing the calculation and presentation of performance; GIPS compliance never exempts a firm from local performance-advertising rules. Where local requirements conflict with the standards, the firm follows the law and discloses the conflict.
rationales.C: In some markets the GIPS standards are so well accepted by plan sponsors and consultants that non-compliance is a serious competitive impediment to a firm's winning new institutional business. Requests for proposals in manager searches routinely ask whether the responding firm is in compliance with the GIPS standards and whether it has been independently verified. The global recognition the standards have gained also helps the compliant firm compete in international markets, and compliance has appropriately been characterized as the investment management firm's passport to the international marketplace. Because the standards reflect best practices in the calculation and presentation of investment performance, firms may also realize internal benefits: implementing them may identify opportunities to strengthen managerial controls, improve oversight of investment operations, give management additional comfort in the accuracy of performance reporting, and improve the quality of information available to the firm through technological enhancements.

questions.stem: The 2020 edition of the GIPS standards is most likely:

options.A: effective as of 1 January 2021.
options.B: effective as of 1 January 2020.
options.C: effective 1 January 2020 under a single consolidated chapter.

rationales.A: The 2020 edition is effective as of 1 January 2020, not 2021. GIPS Reports that include performance for periods ending on or after 31 December 2020 must be prepared in accordance with the 2020 edition, and it is that 31 December 2020 cut-off, rather than any 2021 date, that governs which reports fall under the edition.
rationales.B: The 2020 edition of the GIPS standards is effective as of 1 January 2020. GIPS Reports that include performance for periods ending on or after 31 December 2020 must be prepared in accordance with the 2020 edition. That edition contains three chapters, the GIPS Standards for Firms, the GIPS Standards for Asset Owners, and the GIPS Standards for Verifiers, each with its own glossary.
rationales.C: The 2020 edition contains three separate chapters, each with its own glossary: the GIPS Standards for Firms, the GIPS Standards for Asset Owners, and the GIPS Standards for Verifiers. Provisions were organized by type of entity rather than consolidated into a single chapter applying to firms, asset owners and verifiers alike, which is why a discretionary manager and a non-competing asset owner look to different chapters.

drills.los_text: explain the fundamentals of compliance with the GIPS standards, including the definition of the firm and the firm's definition of discretion
drills.reading_name: Overview of the Global Investment Performance Standards

questions.stem: The fundamentals of compliance in the GIPS Standards for Firms most likely consist of:

options.A: both requirements and recommendations.
options.B: recommendations only, adopted at each firm's discretion.
options.C: requirements only, with no recommendations.

rationales.A: The fundamentals of compliance contain 39 requirements and seven recommendations, so both kinds of provision are present. Several core principles create the foundation for the GIPS standards, including properly defining the firm, providing GIPS Reports to all prospective clients and prospective pooled fund investors, adhering to applicable laws and regulations, and ensuring that information presented is not false or misleading.
rationales.B: The fundamentals of compliance are largely mandatory: 39 of the provisions are requirements and only seven are recommendations. Treating them as discretionary reflects the misconception that all GIPS provisions are voluntary. The decision to claim compliance is voluntary, but once a firm claims compliance the requirements bind it.
rationales.C: The GIPS standards deliberately separate binding requirements from non-binding recommendations, and the fundamentals of compliance contain both: 39 requirements and seven recommendations. A recommendation is best practice that a firm is encouraged, but not obliged, to adopt, so a single undifferentiated body of mandatory provisions does not describe the structure.

questions.stem: For purposes of a claim of GIPS compliance, the firm is most likely defined as:

options.A: any composite, product line, or pooled fund the manager elects to present.
options.B: the entire legal entity, including all parent, affiliated and subsidiary companies.
options.C: the entity held out to the public as a distinct business entity.

rationales.A: GIPS compliance is firm-wide and cannot be claimed for only some of a firm's products, nor for specific composites, pooled funds, or portfolios. The firm must be an investment firm, subsidiary, or division held out to the public as a distinct business entity, not a single composite or product line the manager elects to present.
rationales.B: The firm is the entity held out to the public as a distinct business entity, and it need not be the whole legal entity or corporate group. A distinct business entity is a unit, division, department, or office that is organizationally and functionally segregated from other units, divisions, departments, or offices, that retains discretion over the assets it manages, and that should have autonomy over the investment decision-making process, so a subsidiary or division can be the firm on its own.
rationales.C: The firm must be defined as an investment firm, subsidiary, or division held out to the public as a distinct business entity. A distinct business entity is a unit, division, department, or office that is organizationally and functionally segregated from other units, divisions, departments, or offices and that retains discretion over the assets it manages and that should have autonomy over the investment decision-making process. Possible criteria for identifying a distinct business entity are the organization being a legal entity, having a distinct market or client type, or using a separate and distinct investment process.

questions.stem: A bank's wealth management department comprises a private client division and an institutional division, marketed under separate names, each with its own investment management, trading, marketing, administrative and accounting staff. Only the institutional division elects to implement the GIPS standards. A claim of compliance is most likely available to:

options.A: the institutional division alone.
options.B: both divisions together, as a combined firm.
options.C: the whole bank, including its lending operations.

rationales.A: The institutional division holds itself out to customers as a distinct business unit, with its own autonomous investment management, research, trading, and administrative team, so it may be defined as the firm and may become GIPS-compliant on its own. The illustrative case is a super-regional bank whose wealth management department consists of two separate and distinct divisions: a private client division offering investment management to private individuals and families, and an institutional client division serving tax-exempt non-profit organizations including pension funds and charitable foundations, which does not solicit or handle non-institutional business. Each division has its own investment management team, traders, marketing department, administrative personnel, and accounting department. The institutional unit decides to achieve compliance with the GIPS standards while the private client division makes a business decision not to implement them, and that split is permissible precisely because each division is a distinct business entity. Compliance then applies firm-wide within the institutional division.
rationales.B: Divisions that are held out to the market as distinct business entities may each be defined as a separate firm, so there is no requirement to combine them into one GIPS firm. What matters is organizational and functional segregation from other units, retained discretion over the assets managed, and autonomy over the investment decision-making process; separate names alone neither forces nor forbids combination.
rationales.C: The firm is defined as the entity held out to clients as a distinct business entity, here a wealth management division, not the whole bank or its holding company, and lending operations are not discretionary investment management at all. Compliance must be firm-wide for the entity as defined, which is why the institutional division must comply across all of its own products, but it need not extend to the private client division or to the bank's other businesses.

questions.stem: Under the GIPS standards, total firm assets are most likely measured as:

options.A: the fair value of all assets the firm manages.
options.B: the historical cost of all assets the firm manages.
options.C: the fair value of discretionary, fee-paying portfolios only.

rationales.A: Total firm assets refers to the aggregate fair value of all assets for which a firm has investment management responsibility, whether or not those assets are discretionary and whether or not they are fee-paying. The phrase establishes the boundary of the defined firm for GIPS purposes. Total firm assets include assets managed by sub-advisors that the firm has the authority to select, but they do not include advisory-only assets or uncalled committed capital. Two features define the measure: the basis is fair value rather than cost, and the test for inclusion is investment management responsibility rather than composite eligibility.
rationales.B: The basis of measurement is aggregate fair value, not historical cost. Fair value is what makes reported firm size and composite assets comparable from firm to firm and comparable with the performance figures presented alongside them; historical cost would not reflect the current value of the assets the firm is responsible for managing, and the subjectivity that cost accounting avoids is handled instead by the valuation requirements and disclosures the standards impose.
rationales.C: Total firm assets cover all assets under the firm's investment management responsibility, discretionary or not and fee-paying or not. The narrower discretionary, fee-paying test governs composite inclusion, not total firm assets: both discretionary and non-discretionary portfolios are counted in total firm assets, while only discretionary portfolios are included in composites. Restricting the aggregate to composite-eligible portfolios would understate the firm and defeat the purpose of the measure, which is to show the whole of what the firm manages.

questions.stem: After a change in a firm's corporate structure or organizational design, its historical performance is most likely:

options.A: left unaltered.
options.B: left to the firm's discretion.
options.C: restated to reflect the new structure.

rationales.A: A firm that has been defined for the purposes of the GIPS standards may well undergo subsequent changes in its corporate structure or organizational design. Changes in a firm's organization are not permitted to lead to alteration of historical performance, however. As a general rule, apart from correcting errors, historical performance is not to be altered. The record belongs to the composite and to the periods in which the return was actually earned, so a reorganization carries that record forward unchanged.
rationales.B: The standards are not silent on this point and the treatment is not discretionary. They address organizational change directly and require that historical performance survive it: apart from the correction of errors, history is not to be altered. Leaving the question to each firm's judgment would let a firm reshape its record every time it reorganized, which is precisely the outcome the rule forecloses.
rationales.C: Restating history to match a new corporate structure is what the standards prohibit. Changes in a firm's organization are not permitted to lead to alteration of historical composite performance; only the correction of errors may change a record that has already been reported.

questions.stem: Composite inclusion of a firm's discretionary, fee-paying segregated accounts is most likely:

options.A: required for the ten largest only.
options.B: required for all such accounts.
options.C: optional for every such account.

rationales.A: The requirement is universal across qualifying accounts rather than ranked by size. All discretionary, fee-paying segregated accounts must be included in at least one composite, and nothing in the standards limits that obligation to the largest accounts. A size cut-off would let a firm omit the qualifying accounts it preferred not to show, which is the result the requirement exists to prevent.
rationales.B: The GIPS Standards for Firms require that all discretionary, fee-paying segregated accounts be included in at least one composite. Discretionary, fee-paying pooled funds must also be included in at least one composite if they meet a composite definition. The key term in the requirement is discretionary, although the GIPS standards do not define the term itself. Generally speaking, a portfolio is discretionary if the manager is able to implement the intended investment strategy. Although both discretionary and non-discretionary portfolios are included in total firm assets, only discretionary portfolios are included in composites. Where a client imposes restrictions on the manager's freedom to buy, hold and sell securities so as to carry out the strategy and achieve the portfolio's financial objectives, the manager must consider whether the portfolio is in fact discretionary. In general, restrictions that impede the investment process to such an extent that the strategy cannot be implemented as intended may be presumed to render the portfolio non-discretionary, and such a portfolio should not be included in a composite.
rationales.C: Inclusion is not optional. All discretionary, fee-paying segregated accounts must be included in at least one composite, and that requirement is what stops a firm from selecting which accounts a prospective client sees presented on their own. A firm may of course show an individual portfolio in addition to its composite presentation, but it cannot keep a qualifying account out of every composite.

questions.stem: The requirements grouped under Fundamentals of Compliance are most likely to address:

options.A: the minimum number of years needed to initially claim compliance.
options.B: a uniform fee schedule for compliant firms.
options.C: a required portfolio accounting system.

rationales.A: The other requirements under Fundamentals of Compliance can be broadly characterized as relating to: the minimum number of years required in order to initially claim compliance with the GIPS standards; documenting policies and procedures related to compliance; complying with laws and regulations; avoiding false or misleading performance and performance-related information; the requirements concerning the distribution of GIPS Reports and of lists of firm composites and pooled funds; the use of total return benchmarks reflective of the investment strategy; the requirement to correct material errors in a GIPS Report and to redistribute the report to the appropriate parties; the maintenance of the data and information necessary to support the elements of the GIPS Reports; and the conditions under which performance may be used or linked to that of another firm.
rationales.B: The GIPS standards govern the calculation and presentation of investment performance; they do not regulate what a firm charges its clients. Fundamentals of Compliance instead addresses matters such as the minimum number of years needed to initially claim compliance, documented policies and procedures, compliance with applicable laws and regulations, avoiding false or misleading performance information, and the correction of material errors in a GIPS Report. Fees enter the standards only through requirements on gross-of-fees and net-of-fees return presentation and disclosure, never as a prescribed schedule.
rationales.C: No particular portfolio accounting or performance system is mandated. The fundamentals of compliance cover the conditions for claiming compliance, the distribution of GIPS Reports and of composite and pooled fund lists, the use of total return benchmarks, the avoidance of false or misleading information, and the maintenance of the data and records needed to support a GIPS Report. The standards specify the outcomes a firm must be able to produce and support, and leave the choice of system to the firm.

questions.stem: When the GIPS standards conflict with local laws on the calculation and presentation of performance, a firm is most likely required to:

options.A: withdraw its claim of compliance.
options.B: follow the law and disclose the conflict.
options.C: follow the GIPS standards rather than the law.

rationales.A: The claim of compliance continues. The standards anticipate conflicts with law and resolve them without requiring a firm to abandon compliance: the firm complies with the law or regulation and discloses the conflict in the GIPS Report. Firms are strongly encouraged to comply with the GIPS standards in addition to applicable regulatory requirements, so the appropriate response is disclosure rather than withdrawal.
rationales.B: When the GIPS standards conflict with laws or regulations regarding the calculation and presentation of performance, the GIPS standards obligate firms to comply with the laws and regulations and to disclose the conflict in the GIPS Report. The disclosure is what keeps the report honest: a reader learns that a presented figure departs from a GIPS provision and why it does. Firms are strongly encouraged to comply with the GIPS standards in addition to applicable regulatory requirements.
rationales.C: Compliance with the GIPS standards is voluntary and cannot displace binding law. Where the two conflict, the firm must comply with the law or regulation and disclose the conflict in the GIPS Report, so the local requirement prevails over the conflicting GIPS provision. The voluntary character of the standards is the reason they yield, not a reason they override.

drills.los_text: discuss requirements of the GIPS standards with respect to return calculation methodologies, including the treatment of external cash flows, cash and cash equivalents, and expenses and fees
drills.reading_name: Overview of the Global Investment Performance Standards

questions.stem: Under the GIPS standards, the return a firm must present for a portfolio is most likely:

options.A: the money-weighted return in all cases.
options.B: the time-weighted return.
options.C: either return, at the firm's discretion.

rationales.A: This inverts the rule. The GIPS standards mandate the time-weighted return; the money-weighted return may be used only for portfolios meeting certain conditions, which makes it the exception rather than the required measure. A money-weighted return reflects the timing and size of external cash flows, which in most mandates the client controls, so it is not a fair basis for comparing managers.
rationales.B: The GIPS standards mandate the use of a time-weighted return (TWR); money-weighted returns may be used for portfolios meeting certain conditions. TWR is a method of calculating period-by-period returns that reflects the change in value and negates the effects of external cash flows, which is what makes it comparable across managers who do not control the timing of client flows. Except for private market investment portfolios, portfolios using TWR must be valued monthly and the TWR must be calculated at least monthly, as of the calendar month end or the last business day of the month. If returns are not calculated daily and the portfolio receives an intra-month large cash flow, the portfolio must be valued and a sub-period return must be calculated at the time of the large cash flow. Private market investment portfolios (real estate and infrastructure, private equity and similar investments that are illiquid, not publicly traded and not traded on an exchange) must be valued quarterly.
rationales.C: The choice is not free. A time-weighted return is required unless the firm has control over the external cash flows and either the portfolio is closed-end, fixed life or fixed commitment, or illiquid investments are a significant part of the investment strategy. Absent those conditions the firm must present a time-weighted return, and a firm that could pick its method at will could pick the more flattering one.

questions.stem: The definition of a large cash flow is most likely:

options.A: set by the firm for each composite.
options.B: set by the flow's effect on composite membership.
options.C: set by the GIPS standards as a fixed percentage of assets.

rationales.A: What constitutes a large cash flow is defined by the firm. It is usually an external cash flow of such size that it may distort the return if the portfolio is not valued and a sub-period return is not calculated at the time of the cash flow. A large cash flow may be defined either relative to an absolute monetary threshold or as a percentage of the portfolio or composite assets. The GIPS standards do not specify a quantitative definition of large external cash flows: taking into account the liquidity of the market segments or asset classes and the nature of the investment strategy, firms must make their own determinations for each composite.
rationales.B: A large cash flow is about distortion of a measured return, not about which composite a portfolio belongs to. The size of the flow matters because it obliges the firm to value the portfolio and calculate a sub-period return at the date of the flow when returns are not calculated daily. Whether a portfolio continues to fit a composite definition is a separate question, governed by that definition and by the firm's policies on including and removing portfolios.
rationales.C: The GIPS standards deliberately prescribe no quantitative threshold, whether as a percentage of assets or otherwise. The firm defines what constitutes a large cash flow for each composite, taking account of the liquidity of the market segments or asset classes involved and the nature of the investment strategy, and it may express the definition either as an absolute monetary amount or as a percentage of portfolio or composite assets. A single prescribed figure would be too coarse to work across liquid and illiquid strategies alike.

questions.stem: Presenting a money-weighted return in place of a time-weighted return is most likely:

options.A: permitted for qualifying portfolios whose cash flows the firm controls.
options.B: permitted whenever the firm prefers the resulting figure.
options.C: prohibited under the GIPS standards.

rationales.A: A firm may choose to present money-weighted returns (MWRs) instead of time-weighted returns if the firm has control over the external cash flows and either (1) the portfolios are closed-end, fixed life or fixed commitment, or (2) illiquid investments are a significant part of the investment strategy. Annualized, since-inception MWRs must be calculated at least annually. For periods beginning with the effective date of the 2020 GIPS Standards, daily external cash flows must be used; external cash flows for periods prior to that date must be reflected on at least a quarterly basis. Portfolios for which a money-weighted return is calculated must be valued at least annually and as of the period end for which performance is calculated.
rationales.B: The permission is conditioned on the firm's control over external cash flows and on the characteristics of the portfolio, never on which figure presents the record more favorably. A firm free to switch methods in order to flatter a result would defeat the comparability the standards exist to create, and the conditions attached to money-weighted reporting, along with the valuation and cash flow requirements that come with it, are what keep the choice principled.
rationales.C: Money-weighted returns are permitted, though only in defined circumstances: the firm must have control over the external cash flows, and either the portfolio must be closed-end, fixed life or fixed commitment, or illiquid investments must be a significant part of the strategy. Where the manager controls the timing of the flows, the money-weighted return is the more informative measure, because the manager is accountable for that timing.

questions.stem: A portfolio is worth $100,000 on 31 May and $110,550 on 30 June, and is worth $109,000 on 5 June after receiving a $10,000 contribution that day. For June, the portfolio's true time-weighted return is most likely:

options.A: below its Modified Dietz return.
options.B: equal to its Modified Dietz return.
options.C: not determinable from the data given.

rationales.A: The true time-weighted return using the intra-period valuation method is 0.41%. The month splits at the contribution date: the first sub-period return is (109,000 - 10,000 - 100,000)/100,000 = -0.01, the second is (110,550 - 109,000)/109,000 = 0.0142, and compounding gives (1 + -0.01)(1 + 0.0142) - 1 = 0.0041, or 0.41%. Modified Dietz instead weights the flow by the fraction of the period for which it was held: w = (CD - D)/CD = (30 - 5)/30 = 25/30 = 0.83, so the return is (110,550 - 100,000 - 10,000)/[100,000 + (10,000 x 25/30)] = 550/108,333.33 = 0.0051, or 0.51%. The Modified IRR method applied to the same data also gives 0.51%. The true time-weighted return is therefore the lower of the two, because the approximation methods do not recognize that the portfolio had already lost value before the contribution arrived, and so they credit the loss to a smaller effective base.
rationales.B: The two methods do not agree here, and in general they coincide only when there is no external cash flow within the period. Modified Dietz approximates the return by weighting the flow for the time it was held rather than valuing the portfolio at the flow date and compounding sub-period returns. On these figures the approximation gives 0.51% against a true time-weighted return of 0.41%, a gap of 10 basis points in a single month. The approximation is why the standards require a valuation and a sub-period return at the date of a large cash flow when returns are not calculated daily.
rationales.C: The data are sufficient. A valuation at the cash flow date is exactly what the true time-weighted return calls for, and the 5 June value of $109,000 supplies it: the month is divided into the periods before and after the contribution, a return is computed for each, and the two are compounded to 0.41%. A mid-period external flow makes the calculation longer, not impossible, and it is the reason the intra-period valuation method exists.

questions.stem: Returns on cash and cash equivalents held in a portfolio are most likely:

options.A: reported separately from total return.
options.B: included in all total return calculations.
options.C: excluded when another firm manages the cash.

rationales.A: Cash returns are not carved out and shown on their own. Because an active manager, within the constraints established by the client's investment policy statement, often has discretion over what portion of the portfolio to hold in cash or cash equivalents, the portfolio's return is affected by that decision. The contribution of cash and cash equivalents must therefore be reflected within every total return calculation rather than presented alongside it, so that the reported return is the return the client actually earned on the whole portfolio.
rationales.B: Returns from cash and cash equivalents held in portfolios must be included in all total return calculations. A primary purpose of performance measurement is to enable prospective clients and, by extension, their consultants to evaluate an investment management firm's results. Within the constraints established by a client's investment policy statement (IPS), active managers often have discretion to decide what portion of a portfolio's assets to hold in cash or cash equivalents. The portfolio return will be affected by how much cash the manager elects to hold, and thus return calculations must reflect the contribution of the cash and cash equivalents to investment results. Even if the management of cash balances is handled by another firm, as is often the case in manager-of-manager arrangements, cash and cash equivalents must be included in the total return calculation.
rationales.C: Delegating the management of cash balances changes nothing. Even when cash is handled by another firm, as is often the case in manager-of-manager arrangements, cash and cash equivalents must still be included in the total return calculation, because the decision to hold that cash affects the result the client received. Excluding delegated cash would let a firm report the return on its selected securities while setting aside the drag or benefit of the cash position that accompanied them.

questions.stem: Under the GIPS standards, annualizing a return for a period of less than one year is most likely:

options.A: prohibited.
options.B: permitted if the methodology is disclosed.
options.C: required.

rationales.A: Returns for periods of less than one year must not be annualized. Extrapolating partial-year returns by annualizing them would amount to a prediction about investment results for the rest of the year, which is not a return the firm has actually earned and may not be presented as one.
rationales.B: Disclosure does not cure the problem. Annualizing a partial-year return amounts to predicting results for the remainder of the year, so annualization is prohibited outright for periods of less than one year, whatever methodology is disclosed alongside it.
rationales.C: The requirement is the opposite: returns for periods of less than one year must not be annualized, because extrapolating them embeds a forecast of the remaining months. Comparability with an annual benchmark is achieved by presenting the partial period as a partial period, not by scaling it up to a full year.

questions.stem: Under the GIPS standards, the treatment of transaction costs and bundled fees is most likely that:

options.A: returns are calculated before deducting transaction costs.
options.B: per-transaction custody fees are transaction costs.
options.C: returns are calculated after deducting transaction costs.

rationales.A: The GIPS standards require that returns be calculated after the deduction of transaction costs incurred during the period. Presenting a return that still includes those costs, with a separate disclosure of them, does not satisfy the requirement.
rationales.B: Custody fees are not transaction costs, even when they are charged on a per-transaction basis. Transaction costs are the costs of buying or selling investments: brokerage commissions, exchange fees and/or taxes, or spreads from internal or external brokers.
rationales.C: Returns must be calculated after the deduction of transaction costs incurred during the period. Transaction costs are the costs of buying or selling investments, and typically take the form of brokerage commissions, exchange fees and/or taxes, or spreads from either internal or external brokers. Custody fees should not be considered transaction costs, even when they are charged on a per-transaction basis. Some portfolios pay bundled fees, which can include any combination of investment management fees, transaction costs, custody fees, and/or administrative fees. If transaction costs cannot be identified — either actual transaction costs or estimated costs based on a reasonable estimation method — and segregated from a bundled fee, composites for institutional investors must reduce the gross-of-fees return by the entire amount of the bundled fee, or by that portion of the bundled fee that includes the transaction costs.

drills.los_text: explain the recommended valuation hierarchy of the GIPS standards
drills.reading_name: Overview of the Global Investment Performance Standards

questions.stem: Under the GIPS standards, fair value is most likely the:

options.A: amortized acquisition cost of the investment.
options.B: price a distressed seller would accept in a forced liquidation.
options.C: amount realizable in an orderly, arm's-length transaction.

rationales.A: Firms are required to apply a fair value methodology, not a historical or amortized cost methodology. Acquisition cost adjusted for amortization and impairment is an accounting cost measurement, and confusing it with fair value is a common error.
rationales.B: Fair value assumes an orderly, arm's-length transaction between willing parties. A forced or distressed liquidation is neither orderly nor between willing parties, so the price obtained in one is not fair value.
rationales.C: Firms are required to apply a fair value methodology when valuing assets. The GIPS standards define fair value as the amount at which an investment could be sold in an orderly, arm's-length transaction between willing parties. The valuation must be determined using the objective, observable, unadjusted quoted market price for an identical investment in an active market on the measurement date, if available. Fair value must include any accrued income on fixed-income securities and on all other investments that earn interest income; a firm may choose to recognize income on cash and cash equivalents on a cash basis rather than an accrual basis.

questions.stem: The input at the top of the GIPS recommended valuation hierarchy is most likely the:

options.A: firm's internal model price.
options.B: quoted price for an identical investment in an active market.
options.C: quoted price for a similar investment in an active market.

rationales.A: Model prices sit at the bottom of the hierarchy: subjective, unobservable inputs are the least-preferred level, used only when nothing observable is available or appropriate. Objective, observable market prices come first, however well a firm knows its own holdings.
rationales.B: The top of the hierarchy is the objective, observable, unadjusted quoted market price for an identical investment in an active market on the measurement date. If such a price is available it must be used, so it takes precedence over every other valuation approach.
rationales.C: Quoted prices for similar investments in active markets are the next level down — the first recommended alternative, used only when a quoted price for an identical investment in an active market is not available. Identical-investment quoted prices top the hierarchy.

questions.stem: When quoted prices for identical investments in active markets are unavailable, the first alternative in the GIPS recommended valuation hierarchy is most likely:

options.A: quoted prices for similar investments in active markets.
options.B: subjective, unobservable inputs from the firm's models.
options.C: the most recent transaction price for the investment.

rationales.A: If objective, observable, unadjusted quoted market prices for identical investments in active markets on the measurement date are not available, the recommended alternatives, in declining order of preference, are: (1) quoted prices for similar investments in active markets; (2) quoted prices for identical or similar investments in markets that are not active — markets in which there are few transactions for the investment, prices are not current, or price quotations vary substantially over time and/or between market makers; (3) market-based inputs, other than quoted prices, that are observable for the investment; and (4) subjective, unobservable inputs. Each level is used only if the inputs above it are not available or appropriate.
rationales.B: Subjective, unobservable inputs are the lowest and least-preferred level of the hierarchy, reached only when none of the observable alternatives above them are available or appropriate. Putting them first inverts the recommended order.
rationales.C: A transaction price from a market that is not currently active belongs to the second alternative — quoted prices for identical or similar investments in markets that are not active, where there are few transactions, prices are not current, or quotations vary substantially. The first alternative is quoted prices for similar investments in active markets.

questions.stem: Within the GIPS recommended valuation hierarchy, subjective, unobservable inputs most likely rank:

options.A: highest.
options.B: intermediate.
options.C: lowest.

rationales.A: Subjective, unobservable inputs sit at the bottom of the hierarchy, not the top. The highest-preference input is the objective, observable, unadjusted quoted market price for an identical investment in an active market on the measurement date, which must be used if available.
rationales.B: They are the least-preferred input of all, ranking below market-based observable inputs other than quoted prices, so they do not sit in the middle of the hierarchy.
rationales.C: Subjective, unobservable inputs are the lowest level of the recommended valuation hierarchy, used to value an investment only when no observable inputs are available or appropriate. Above them, in declining order of preference: (1) the objective, observable, unadjusted quoted market price for an identical investment in an active market, which must be used if available; (2) quoted prices for similar investments in active markets; (3) quoted prices for identical or similar investments in markets that are not active; and (4) market-based inputs other than quoted prices that are observable for the investment.

questions.stem: Under the GIPS standards, the recommended scope of a firm's valuation hierarchy is most likely:

options.A: limited to private-market composites.
options.B: specific to each composite or pooled fund.
options.C: uniform across all composites and pooled funds.

rationales.A: The requirement to document valuation policies, procedures, methodologies, and hierarchies applies to the firm as a whole, and the recommendation that hierarchies be composite- or pooled fund-specific is not confined to private markets. Illiquid strategies such as real estate and private equity are the clearest cases for a tailored hierarchy, but the recommendation is not restricted to them.
rationales.B: The GIPS standards not only require firms to document their valuation policies, procedures, methodologies, and hierarchies but also recommend that the valuation hierarchies be composite- or pooled fund-specific. Normally, for investment strategies that employ plain-vanilla securities trading in robust markets, quoted prices are readily available. Other composites, however, may represent strategies that materially make use of securities that trade infrequently in relatively illiquid markets, where values must be imputed or estimated; real estate and private equity are obvious examples.
rationales.C: The recommendation is that hierarchies be appropriate to — and so may be specific to — individual composites or pooled funds. A plain-vanilla equity composite priced off active markets and an illiquid real estate composite whose values must be imputed do not face the same valuation inputs, so one rigid firm-wide hierarchy is not required.

questions.stem: Under the GIPS standards, valuation policies, once established, most likely:

options.A: must be documented and available to clients on request.
options.B: may vary by period without documentation.
options.C: need not be shared with prospective clients.

rationales.A: Once established, the valuation policies must be documented, followed consistently, and made available to prospective clients upon request. For assets valued using quantitative models, it is useful to list input factors such as discount rates and risk-adjusted cash flow projections and to review the basis for estimating them. Portfolio managers, security analysts, quantitative analysts, and traders should participate in those discussions.
rationales.B: Once established, policies must be documented and followed consistently. They cannot be shifted from period to period as market conditions change, and they certainly cannot be left undocumented.
rationales.C: Valuation policies must be made available to prospective clients upon request, so they are not purely internal working documents.

drills.los_text: explain requirements of the GIPS standards with respect to composite return calculations, including methods for asset-weighting portfolio returns
drills.reading_name: Overview of the Global Investment Performance Standards

questions.stem: Under the GIPS standards, a permitted method of calculating a composite time-weighted return most likely weights the individual portfolio returns:

options.A: equally.
options.B: by ending-period values.
options.C: by beginning-of-period values.

rationales.A: Equal weighting of the individual portfolio returns is not permitted, because it ignores the size of each portfolio in the composite. Composite returns must be calculated by asset-weighting the individual portfolio returns using beginning-of-period values, by a method that reflects both beginning-of-period values and external cash flows, or by the Aggregate Return method.
rationales.B: Weighting by ending-period values is not one of the three permitted approaches. The standards specify beginning-of-period asset weighting, a method that reflects both beginning-of-period values and external cash flows, or the Aggregate Return method.
rationales.C: Time-weighted composite returns must be calculated in one of three ways: (1) asset-weighting the individual portfolio returns using beginning-of-period values; (2) using a method that reflects both beginning-of-period values and external cash flows; or (3) using the Aggregate Return method.

questions.stem: Under the beginning assets weighting method, a composite return is most likely calculated by weighting each portfolio's return by:

options.A: an equal share of the composite.
options.B: its share of aggregate beginning fair value.
options.C: its share of aggregate ending market value.

rationales.A: A simple arithmetic average of the constituent returns ignores portfolio size. The beginning assets method asset-weights those returns in proportion to their respective percentages of aggregate beginning assets.
rationales.B: Under the beginning assets weighting method, r_C = Σ [r_pi × (V_0,pi / Σ V_0,pi)], where r_C is the composite return, r_pi is the return of an individual portfolio i, V_0,pi is the beginning value of portfolio i, and Σ V_0,pi is the total beginning fair value of all the individual portfolios in the composite. In other words, the composite return is the sum of the individual portfolio returns weighted in proportion to their respective percentages of aggregate beginning assets.
rationales.C: The weights are the beginning-of-period fair values of the portfolios, not their ending values. Weighting by ending values would let within-period performance and external cash flows determine the weights applied to the returns those same flows helped produce.

questions.stem: A composite's constituent portfolios experienced external cash flows during the measurement period. Under the GIPS standards, each portfolio's return is most likely weighted by its:

options.A: beginning assets plus day-weighted external cash flows.
options.B: equal share of an unweighted average.
options.C: beginning-of-period assets alone.

rationales.A: Under the beginning assets plus weighted cash flows method, the composite return is r_C = Σ [r_pi × (V_pi / Σ V_pi)], where V_pi = V_0 + Σ(CF_i × w_i) is the sum of beginning assets and weighted external cash flows for portfolio i. That same V_pi is the denominator of the Modified Dietz formula. Cash flows are weighted by w_i = (CD − D_i)/CD, where CD is the total number of calendar days in the period and D_i is the number of calendar days from the beginning of the period to the time the cash flow occurs. This method uses the individual portfolios' V_pi in place of V_0,p, so a portfolio that received a large contribution early in the period carries a correspondingly larger weight in the composite.
rationales.B: Composite returns must be asset-weighted, not equally weighted. An equally weighted arithmetic average of the individual portfolio returns ignores portfolio size entirely, so a small portfolio would influence the reported composite return as much as one many times its size, and the composite would not reflect the constituent portfolios' aggregate performance.
rationales.C: Weighting by V_0,pi alone is the beginning-assets method: r_C = Σ [r_pi × (V_0,pi / Σ V_0,pi)], which makes no adjustment for external cash flows. The beginning assets plus weighted cash flows method instead uses V_pi = V_0 + Σ(CF_i × w_i) in the weight, so contributions and withdrawals during the period, weighted by the time they were in the portfolio, do affect each portfolio's weight.

questions.stem: A composite contains four portfolios with beginning fair values of $100.00K, $97.40K, $112.94K, and $124.47K (total $434.81K) and ending fair values of $110.55K, $105.20K, $113.30K, and $100.50K (total $429.55K). Under the beginning-of-period asset-weighting method, the weight assigned to the portfolio that begins at $100.00K is closest to:

rationales.A: 26% is what weighting by ending fair values produces: 110.55/429.55 = 0.257. The beginning-of-period asset-weighting method uses beginning fair values, giving 100/434.81 = 0.23, or 23%.
rationales.B: 25% is the equal, one-of-four weight. The method asset-weights each portfolio by its beginning fair value rather than weighting the four portfolios equally, giving 100/434.81 = 0.23, or 23%.
rationales.C: The four portfolios begin at $100.00K, $97.40K, $112.94K, and $124.47K and end at $110.55K, $105.20K, $113.30K, and $100.50K; the combined beginning fair value is $434.81K and the combined ending fair value is $429.55K. The first portfolio has a beginning fair value of $100,000 and all four portfolios combined have a beginning fair value of approximately $435,000, so under beginning-of-period weighting the weight assigned to it is 100/434.81 = 0.23, or 23%. Determining a composite return when there are external cash flows is more complex: the cash flows must be weighted following the methodology used in the Modified Dietz rate-of-return calculation, w_i = (CD − D_i)/CD.

questions.stem: Under the GIPS standards, the required calculation frequency for composite time-weighted returns, other than for private market investment composites, is most likely:

options.A: annual.
options.B: unspecified.
options.C: monthly.

rationales.A: Annual calculation falls short of the requirement. Composite time-weighted returns, except for private market investment composites, must be calculated at least monthly, and asset-weighting the constituent portfolios only once a year would leave the composite return a poor reflection of their aggregate performance.
rationales.B: A minimum frequency is specified rather than left to the firm: composite time-weighted returns, except for private market investment composites, must be calculated at least monthly. A firm may calculate more frequently, but not less.
rationales.C: Composite time-weighted returns, except for private market investment composites, must be calculated at least monthly. The less frequently the asset-weighting exercise is conducted, the greater the likelihood that composite returns will inaccurately reflect the constituent portfolios' aggregate performance, because weights set long before the period end no longer correspond to the assets actually at risk.

questions.stem: Under the GIPS standards, whether one of a firm's portfolios must be included in a composite is most likely determined by:

options.A: whether a committee deems it representative.
options.B: whether the client consents to performance disclosure.
options.C: whether it is actual, fee-paying, and discretionary.

rationales.A: Inclusion is definition-based, not a matter of annual selection by a performance committee. Requiring every actual, fee-paying, discretionary portfolio to sit in at least one composite is precisely what stops a firm from showing prospective clients only the portfolios that happen to look representative, or best.
rationales.B: Inclusion is mandatory for all actual, fee-paying, discretionary portfolios that meet a composite definition; client consent to performance disclosure is not a filter. Treating consent as a filter would let a firm suppress its weakest results.
rationales.C: To prevent firms from presenting only their best-performing portfolios to prospective clients, the GIPS standards require all actual, fee-paying, discretionary segregated accounts to be included in at least one composite. All actual, fee-paying, discretionary pooled funds must also be included in at least one composite if they meet a composite definition. Non-discretionary segregated accounts and pooled funds must not be included in composites. Non-fee-paying discretionary segregated accounts and pooled funds may be included, but additional disclosures may be required. If a strategy is offered as both a pooled fund and a segregated account, the pooled fund must be included in a composite for that strategy; a firm does not need to create a composite for a strategy offered only as a pooled fund.

questions.stem: A portfolio receives a $10,000 contribution on 5 June, within a measurement period of 30 calendar days, and the firm's policy assumes cash flows occur at the end of the day. Under the Modified Dietz day-weighting convention, the weighting factor applied to this contribution is closest to:

rationales.A: 0.50 assumes the cash flow arrives at mid-period, which is a simplifying convention the Modified Dietz day-weighting does not use. The weight is set by the actual days the money is in the portfolio: w_i = (30 − 5)/30 = 25/30 = 0.83.
rationales.B: The cash flow weight is w_i = (CD − D_i)/CD, where CD is the total number of calendar days in the period and D_i is the number of calendar days from the beginning of the period until cash flow CF_i occurs; the formula assumes cash flows occur at the end of the day. The $10,000 contribution occurs on 5 June, so D_i = 5, and the period has 30 days, so CD = 30. The proportion of the measurement period for which the $10,000 is in the portfolio is w_i = (CD − D_i)/CD = (30 − 5)/30 = 25/30 = 0.83. A firm must apply its policy for weighting cash flows consistently.
rationales.C: 0.17 is D_i/CD = 5/30, which inverts the numerator and measures the part of the period before the contribution arrived. The weight is (CD − D_i)/CD = (30 − 5)/30 = 25/30 = 0.83, the fraction of the period for which the money was actually in the portfolio.

drills.los_text: explain the meaning of "discretionary" in the context of composite construction and, given a description of the relevant facts, determine whether a portfolio is likely to be considered discretionary
drills.reading_name: Overview of the Global Investment Performance Standards

questions.stem: Under the GIPS standards, a portfolio is most likely discretionary if:

options.A: it carries no client-imposed restrictions at all.
options.B: the manager can implement the intended strategy.
options.C: the firm holds full legal power of attorney.

rationales.A: Restrictions render a portfolio non-discretionary only where they impede the investment process to such an extent that the strategy cannot be implemented as intended. Not every client-imposed restriction removes discretion, so freedom from all restrictions is a far stricter test than the standards apply.
rationales.B: Generally speaking, a portfolio is discretionary if the manager is able to implement the intended investment strategy. Restrictions that impede the investment process to such an extent that the strategy cannot be implemented as intended may be presumed to render the portfolio non-discretionary, and it should not then be included in a composite. Because discretion is the key variable that determines inclusion in or exclusion from a composite, a firm implementing the GIPS standards must have a clear, written definition of discretion, and it must apply that definition consistently.
rationales.C: Discretion under the GIPS standards turns on the manager's ability to implement the intended investment strategy, not on the legal authority the client has granted over the account. A firm can hold broad legal authority and still be unable to execute the strategy, and it can lack power of attorney while implementing the mandate in full.

questions.stem: A client's investment policy screens out alcohol, tobacco, and gaming securities, prohibits the sale of company stock, and reflects a statutory bar on non-domestic holdings. Under the GIPS standards, these restrictions are most likely:

options.A: treated as automatically removing discretion.
options.B: assessed for their material effect on the strategy.
options.C: disregarded in the discretion assessment.

rationales.A: None of these constraints automatically renders a portfolio non-discretionary. Each is evaluated for its materiality to implementation of the intended strategy, and a restriction that does not materially affect the manager's ability to execute the mandate leaves the portfolio discretionary.
rationales.B: Some clients may have environmental, social, or governance (ESG) restrictions that prohibit investment in securities issued by companies operating in the alcohol, tobacco, or gaming industries. Others might have restrictions that prohibit the sale of company stock. Legal restrictions may also apply; a public fund, for instance, might be statutorily precluded from investing in non-domestic securities. None of these constraints automatically renders a portfolio non-discretionary. Rather, the portfolio manager must determine whether the client-imposed constraints are likely to materially affect her ability to execute the investment strategy. If the constraints are determined not to have a material effect, the manager could include the portfolio in a composite with portfolios that have no such restriction. If a constraint is material, the manager may include the portfolio in a composite with other, similarly constrained portfolios, or classify it as non-discretionary and exclude the portfolio from all composites.
rationales.C: ESG and similar restrictions are genuine investment constraints rather than mere expressions of client values, and they cannot be set aside when discretion is assessed. The question in each case is whether the restriction materially impedes the intended strategy.

questions.stem: A client directs that legacy holdings with a low cost basis must not be sold, because of the adverse tax consequences of realizing large gains. For composite purposes, this direction most likely:

options.A: bears on discretion if it hinders the strategy.
options.B: has no bearing on the discretion assessment.
options.C: leaves the portfolio discretionary in every case.

rationales.A: A client could insist that the manager retain specific holdings that might not otherwise be held, as when legacy holdings with a low cost basis must not be sold because of the adverse tax consequences of realizing large gains. Retaining the asset may skew performance, and whether the impact is favorable or unfavorable in any given measurement period, the outcome would not reflect the results of the manager's actual discretionary investment management. If holding the assets hinders the manager's ability to implement the intended strategy, either the entire portfolio should be considered non-discretionary and excluded from the firm's composites, or the individual assets should be removed and the remaining assets over which the manager has full discretion should be included in the composite. Alternatively, the firm might include a materiality threshold in its policy, enabling it to consider a portfolio discretionary if the non-discretionary assets make up less than a certain percentage of portfolio assets.
rationales.B: A client-directed prohibition on selling can materially impede implementation of the intended strategy, so it bears directly on whether the portfolio is discretionary. That other portfolios also hold legacy positions does not make the constraint irrelevant; what matters is its size and its effect on the strategy.
rationales.C: The effect depends on materiality. A large frozen position can prevent the manager from implementing the intended strategy, in which case the portfolio is non-discretionary, or the restricted assets are carved out and only the assets over which the manager has full discretion enter the composite.

questions.stem: A client's investment policy prohibits the use of futures, swaps, and options. Under the GIPS standards, this prohibition most likely:

options.A: matters only if derivatives are central to the mandate.
options.B: leaves discretion unaffected in every case.
options.C: renders the portfolio non-discretionary in every case.

rationales.A: A client's investment policy might prohibit the use of derivative securities such as futures, swaps, and options, and the firm must then consider whether the restriction is pertinent. If a portfolio manager is managing a domestic mid-cap stock portfolio, the fact that the client prohibits the use of derivatives may be irrelevant, because the manager's typical investment approach simply buys, holds, and sells common stocks. If the use of derivative securities is central to the firm's implementation of the investment mandate, however, then the client's policy may render the portfolio non-discretionary.
rationales.B: Where derivatives are central to the firm's implementation of the investment mandate, the prohibition can render the portfolio non-discretionary, so the restriction is not harmless in every case. Its relevance has to be judged against the strategy actually being run.
rationales.C: The restriction matters only where derivatives are central to the mandate. For a manager whose approach simply buys, holds, and sells common stocks, the prohibition may be irrelevant and the portfolio remains discretionary.

questions.stem: A client frequently makes large withdrawals, on a regular schedule. Under the GIPS standards, this pattern of external cash flows most likely:

options.A: has no effect on the portfolio's discretion.
options.B: requires the portfolio to be classified as discretionary.
options.C: can render the portfolio non-discretionary.

rationales.A: A pattern of large withdrawals can force the manager to carry so much liquidity that the intended strategy cannot be implemented, which makes the portfolio non-discretionary. That external cash flows are outside the manager's control does not make their pattern irrelevant to the discretion assessment; what matters is the constraint the pattern imposes on implementation.
rationales.B: Frequent large withdrawals tend toward the opposite conclusion: the liquidity they force the manager to hold can make the portfolio non-discretionary, not discretionary. Nothing about a withdrawal pattern compels a finding of discretion.
rationales.C: In some cases the pattern of external cash flows might make a portfolio non-discretionary. If a client frequently makes large withdrawals, perhaps on a regular schedule, the portfolio manager might have to maintain such a high level of liquidity that he cannot truly implement the investment strategy as he does for other portfolios with a similar stated investment mandate, objective, or strategy.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about including model, hypothetical, and seed-money portfolios in composites is most accurate?

options.A: Seed-money portfolios are excluded until external fee-paying clients invest.
options.B: Model portfolios may be included if they are labeled as simulated.
options.C: Model and hypothetical portfolios may never be included.

rationales.A: Portfolios funded with the firm's own money are not barred from composites merely because the strategy has yet to attract outside clients. If a firm creates a new strategy and manages portfolios in that strategy with its own assets, sometimes called seed money, it may include those portfolios in the appropriate composites from inception, subject to any presentation and reporting requirements related to the inclusion of non-fee-paying portfolios in composites. The prohibition that does exist attaches to theoretical performance, not to real money the firm has actually put to work in the strategy.
rationales.B: Labeling does not create a route into a composite. No model or hypothetical portfolio may be included in any composite, and firms may not link the theoretical performance of simulated or model portfolios with actual performance. Model, hypothetical, backtested, and simulated returns are all considered theoretical performance; they can be shown as supplemental information but cannot be linked to actual composite or pooled fund returns, however clearly they are described as simulated.
rationales.C: In the process of developing, testing, and refining new investment strategies, firms frequently construct model portfolios and use historical security prices to simulate hypothetical performance in past measurement periods. No model or hypothetical portfolios may be included in any composite, and firms may not link the theoretical performance of simulated or model portfolios with actual performance. Model, hypothetical, backtested, and simulated returns are all considered theoretical performance: they can be shown as supplemental information, but they cannot be linked to actual composite or pooled fund returns. Real portfolios are treated differently. If the firm created a new strategy and managed portfolios in that strategy with its own assets, sometimes called seed money, it could include those portfolios from inception in appropriate composites, subject to any presentation and reporting requirements related to the inclusion of non-fee-paying portfolios in composites.

drills.los_text: explain the role of investment mandates, objectives, or strategies in the construction of composites
drills.reading_name: Overview of the Global Investment Performance Standards

questions.stem: Under the GIPS standards, composites are most likely defined according to:

options.A: similar returns, even across different mandates.
options.B: portfolio size and client type.
options.C: investment mandate, objective, or strategy.

rationales.A: Firms are not permitted to include portfolios with different investment mandates, objectives, or strategies in the same composite, however similar their realized returns happen to be. Return similarity is an outcome rather than a definition, so grouping on it would let a firm assemble composites after the fact out of portfolios that were never managed to a common strategy, which is precisely what the guiding principle of composite definition forbids.
rationales.B: Portfolio size and client type are not the defining basis for a composite. Composites must be defined according to investment mandate, objective, or strategy; groupings built on size or client type would cut across mandates and pull portfolios with different strategies into one composite, producing composites that are neither objectively representative of the firm's products nor consistent with its marketing strategy.
rationales.C: Under the GIPS standards, composites must be defined according to investment mandate, objective, or strategy, and composites must include all portfolios that meet the composite definition. The composite definition, including the detailed criteria that determine the assignment of portfolios to the composite, must be documented in the firm's policies and procedures. Well-defined composites will be objectively representative of the firm's products and consistent with the firm's marketing strategy. It is a guiding principle of composite definition that firms are not permitted to include portfolios with different investment mandates, objectives, or strategies in the same composite.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the composite-definition hierarchy set out in the GIPS standards?

options.A: A required sequence that begins with benchmarks.
options.B: A suggested sequence that begins with investment mandate.
options.C: A single mandatory sequence that every firm must apply unchanged.

rationales.A: Benchmarks sit fourth in the illustrated sequence, not first: investment mandate, then asset classes, then style or strategy, then benchmarks, then risk/return characteristics. The hierarchy moves from the broadest description of what the portfolio is for down to progressively finer distinctions, so starting at the benchmark would invert it and define the product by its yardstick rather than by its mandate.
rationales.B: One possible hierarchy that may be helpful for a firm considering how to define composites runs as follows: investment mandate, asset classes, style or strategy, benchmarks, and risk/return characteristics. A composite based on the investment mandate bears a summary product or strategy description, such as 'Global Equities'. A composite based on the constituent portfolios' asset class, such as equity or fixed income, may also be acceptable; however, asset classes are broadly inclusive, and because generic descriptions are not very informative, asset class composites should be offered only if they are legitimately and meaningfully representative of the firm's products. An asset-class modifier may then indicate the composite's investment style or strategy.
rationales.C: The hierarchy is offered as one possible approach that may be helpful, not as a mandatory template. Firms adapt composite definitions to their own organizational structures, investment processes, and product sets, which is why the standards describe the sequence as a starting point for a firm considering how to define its composites rather than as a prescribed form.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about defining composites by style is most accurate?

options.A: Style is not a permitted basis for defining composites.
options.B: The equity style matrix classifies portfolios by sector and geography.
options.C: Portfolios may be classified according to a defined style.

rationales.A: Style classification is a legitimate and explicitly suggested basis for defining composites. An equity style matrix that classifies portfolios by capitalization and by style might be the starting point for defining a set of composites, and fixed-income portfolios may be classified by a combination of duration and/or market segment that generally aligns with the major fixed-income indexes.
rationales.B: The equity style matrix classifies portfolios along two different dimensions: capitalization, meaning large cap, mid-cap, and small cap; and style, meaning value, core (also called neutral, market oriented, or blend), and growth. Sector and geography are not the axes of that matrix, although geography can enter a composite definition elsewhere, through the investment mandate itself.
rationales.C: Portfolios might also be classified according to a defined style. An equity style matrix that classifies portfolios by capitalization (large cap, mid-cap, and small cap) and by style (value; core, also called neutral, market oriented, or blend; and growth) might be the starting point for defining a set of composites. Fixed-income portfolios may be classified by a combination of duration and/or market segment that generally aligns with the major fixed-income indexes.

questions.stem: Assigning a portfolio to a style category is most appropriately based on:

options.A: money-weighted averages of its holdings' characteristics.
options.B: nothing, because style categories are only marketing constructs.
options.C: the manager's self-declared strategy label.

rationales.A: A portfolio may be assigned to one of the style categories based on the money-weighted averages of pertinent characteristics of the portfolio's holdings. For example, a portfolio holding stocks with an average market capitalization of $5 billion along with a relatively high price-to-earnings multiple, a relatively high price-to-book ratio, and a relatively low dividend yield would likely be identified as a mid-cap growth portfolio. Alternately, the portfolio's historical monthly or quarterly returns might be regressed against the returns of pertinent capital market indexes to determine which style-specific benchmarks best explain the portfolio's performance.
rationales.B: Style-based composite definition is legitimate, and the standards describe how to carry it out. Money-weighted averages of the characteristics of a portfolio's holdings are one recognized assignment basis, and a returns-based regression against pertinent capital market indexes is another, so style categories are observable properties of the portfolio rather than labels invented for marketing purposes.
rationales.C: Assignment is grounded in evidence about the portfolio itself, not in what the manager calls the product.
