The holdings-based route uses money-weighted averages of characteristics such as average market capitalization, price-to-earnings, price-to-book, and dividend yield; the returns-based route regresses the portfolio's historical monthly or quarterly returns against pertinent capital market indexes to see which style-specific benchmarks best explain performance. A self-declared label can be tested against both, and may fail.

questions.stem: In deciding how many composites to maintain, a firm is most likely to:

options.A: maintain a single firm-wide composite.
options.B: build composites representing its distinct strategies.
options.C: create as many composites as possible.

rationales.A: With too few composites, a firm risks overlooking significant differences and grouping diverse portfolios together into a single, overly broad composite subject to a wide dispersion of portfolio returns. One firm-wide composite is the extreme case: it would mask every strategy distinction the firm actually manages to, and its reported return would describe no product a prospective client could buy.
rationales.B: A useful guideline is to build a set of composites that will accurately represent the firm's distinct investment strategies. With too few composites, a firm risks overlooking significant differences and grouping diverse portfolios together into a single, overly broad composite subject to a wide dispersion of portfolio returns. With too many composites, in addition to incurring unnecessary costs, the firm runs the risk of creating narrowly defined groupings that are too much alike in investment strategy, contain too few portfolios or assets to be useful, or compromise client confidentiality. The count therefore follows from the number of genuinely distinct strategies, not from a preference for breadth or granularity.
rationales.C: With too many composites, in addition to incurring unnecessary costs, the firm runs the risk of creating narrowly defined groupings that are too much alike in investment strategy, contain too few portfolios or assets to be useful, or compromise client confidentiality. Granularity is not free, and a composite containing one or two accounts tells a prospective client about those accounts rather than about a strategy.

questions.stem: The first step in a common-sense process for defining composites is most likely to:

options.A: define as many composites as possible.
options.B: review the firm's organizational structure and investment process.
options.C: survey competitors' presentations for comparability.

rationales.A: Proliferating composites at the outset inverts the process and invites cherry-picking, because the firm would then be fitting portfolios to groupings rather than identifying the strategies it genuinely runs. Marketing flexibility is not the objective; a set of composites that accurately represents the firm's distinct investment strategies is.
rationales.B: A workable sequence runs as follows. First, review the firm's organizational structure and investment process to see if distinctive strategies can be readily identified. Second, review the firm's existing marketing materials to determine which strategies are offered as a segregated account, and if possible review marketing materials from competitors and recently received requests for proposals to determine how the industry defines similar products. Third, construct a provisional framework using descriptive captions to identify possible composites. Fourth, taking into consideration the clients' investment policies, test how well the firm's fee-paying, discretionary portfolios would fit the provisional framework. Fifth, review the proposed set of composites to ensure that, in the aggregate, they are likely to satisfy the requirements of the GIPS standards. Sixth, document the composite definitions in detail and circulate them for final review by all affected parties within the firm.
rationales.C: Competitors' materials and recently received requests for proposals do enter the process, but at the second step, as a check on how the industry defines similar products. The starting point is the firm's own organizational structure and investment process, since only that reveals which distinctive strategies the firm actually manages to and therefore which composites it has to define.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about defining composites by benchmark or by risk/return profile is most accurate?

options.A: Benchmark-based composites are permitted when the benchmark reflects the strategy.
options.B: Benchmark-based composites are prohibited.
options.C: Risk/return-based composites are limited to hedge fund strategies.

rationales.A: Firms may also define composites based on the portfolios' benchmarks, as long as the benchmarks reflect the investment strategy and the firm has no other composites with the same characteristics. This approach is particularly appropriate if the portfolios are limited to holding stocks that are held in the index. Portfolios sharing distinctive risk/return profiles may likewise reasonably be grouped together; for example, enhanced index funds with benchmark-specific targeted excess returns and tracking error tolerances might fall into natural groups. Fixed-income composites can be meaningfully defined in many dimensions as well: by asset class or market segment, such as government debt, mortgage-backed securities, convertible bonds, or high-yield bonds; by investment strategy, such as fundamental credit analysis, sector rotation, or interest rate anticipation; or by investment style, such as indexing or core-plus.
rationales.B: Benchmark-based definition is permitted, subject to two conditions: the benchmark must reflect the investment strategy, and the firm must have no other composite with the same characteristics. It is particularly appropriate where the portfolios are limited to holding stocks that are held in the index. A benchmark that is revised over time does not disqualify the approach, since the composite is defined by the strategy the benchmark represents.
rationales.C: Risk/return characteristics are a general definitional basis available to any firm, not a carve-out for hedge funds. The illustration given is a traditional one: enhanced index funds with benchmark-specific targeted excess returns and tracking error tolerances may fall into natural groups that make sensible composites.

drills.los_text: explain requirements of the GIPS standards with respect to composite construction, including switching portfolios among composites, the timing of the inclusion of new portfolios in composites, and the timing of the exclusion of terminated portfolios from composites
drills.reading_name: Overview of the Global Investment Performance Standards

questions.stem: Under the GIPS standards, a new portfolio must be included in the appropriate composite:

options.A: on a timely and consistent basis once under management.
options.B: at the firm's discretion, once performance stabilizes.
options.C: after twelve months under management.

rationales.A: The standards governing composite construction require that composites include new portfolios on a timely and consistent basis after the portfolio comes under management, and firms are required to establish, document, and consistently apply a policy of including new portfolios in the appropriate composites on a timely basis. For many strategies, new portfolios should be included as of the beginning of the next full performance measurement period after the firm receives the funds: if composite returns are calculated monthly and a portfolio is funded on 20 May, the composite should include the new portfolio as of the beginning of June. It may take time to invest the assets of a new portfolio in accordance with the desired strategy, however, particularly when the portfolio is funded in kind or when the securities to be purchased are relatively illiquid, as in some emerging markets. The standards therefore give firms some discretion, but the firm must establish its policy on a composite-by-composite basis and apply it consistently.
rationales.B: Waiting for performance to settle is the abuse the rule is written to prevent, because a firm that chose its inclusion date account by account could admit portfolios that had started well and hold back those that had not. Any discretion the standards allow over timing is exercised in advance, through a documented policy set on a composite-by-composite basis and applied consistently, not after the first returns are known.
rationales.C: No twelve-month waiting period exists. For many strategies the portfolio enters as of the beginning of the next full performance measurement period after the firm receives the funds, so a portfolio funded on 20 May enters a monthly composite as of the beginning of June. Where it genuinely takes time to invest the assets, because the portfolio was funded in kind or the securities are relatively illiquid, the firm's documented policy governs the delay and must be applied consistently to every portfolio in that composite.

questions.stem: Under the GIPS standards, a terminated portfolio is most likely included in the appropriate composite:

options.A: for no historical periods.
options.B: through the termination date, including the final partial period.
options.C: through the last full period of discretionary management.

rationales.A: Removing terminated accounts from composite history would create survivorship bias, leaving a record built only from relationships that lasted. The historical performance of terminated portfolios remains in the appropriate composite, so the composite continues to describe what the strategy delivered at the time rather than what the surviving accounts delivered.
rationales.B: Inclusion runs through the last full measurement period in which the firm had discretion, not through the termination date itself, and the final partial period is excluded. In many cases the firm loses discretion over the portfolio upon being notified of a pending termination, so the periods between notification and the formal termination date are not periods in which the firm was managing the portfolio to the strategy.
rationales.C: A firm must include a terminated portfolio in the historical performance of the appropriate composite through the last full measurement period in which the firm had the discretion to manage the portfolio to the strategy. In many cases, the firm loses its discretion over the portfolio upon being notified of a pending termination, and when that happens it should include the portfolio in the composite through the last full measurement period prior to notification. If a firm that calculates performance monthly is informed on 20 May that its management contract is being terminated effective 31 May and is instructed to stop trading forthwith, the firm should include the portfolio in its composite only through 30 April. The historical performance of terminated portfolios remains in the appropriate composite.

questions.stem: Switching a portfolio from one composite to another is most likely:

options.A: prohibited in all cases.
options.B: allowed at the firm's discretion.
options.C: allowed on a documented mandate change or composite redefinition.

rationales.A: Switches are not barred outright. A portfolio may be moved when there is a documented change in its investment mandate, objective, or strategy, or when the composite is redefined in such a way that the portfolio no longer fits it. What the standards prohibit is the undocumented, discretionary move, not reassignment as such.
rationales.B: Switching requires a documented change in the portfolio's investment mandate, objective, or strategy, or a redefinition of the composite. Discretionary rebalancing of composite membership to make a composite look more representative is prohibited, because a firm able to transfer portfolios at will could re-populate selected composites with whichever portfolios happened to perform best over the measurement period.
rationales.C: The GIPS standards stipulate that portfolios cannot be switched from one composite to another unless documented changes in the portfolio's investment mandate, objective, or strategy, or the redefinition of the composite, make it appropriate. The historical performance of the portfolio must remain with the original composite. This is an important requirement: if the GIPS standards permitted firms to transfer portfolios from one composite to another at will, an unethical firm might identify and exploit opportunities to improve the reported performance of selected composites by re-populating them with the portfolios whose investment results were most advantageous during the measurement period.

questions.stem: Reassignment of a portfolio to a different composite is most likely permitted when:

options.A: the client documents a change in mandate.
options.B: the portfolio's returns diverge from the composite average.
options.C: the firm's verifier gives written approval.

rationales.A: The GIPS standards describe two conditions under which portfolios can be reassigned. First, a portfolio can be switched from one composite to another if the client revises the mandate, objective, or strategy governing the investment of portfolio assets and the guideline changes are documented; a client might decide to modify a portfolio mandate from mid-cap value to large-cap value, or from domestic equity to global equity, while retaining the same investment advisor. Second, a portfolio can be reassigned to another composite if the original composite is redefined in such a way that the portfolio no longer fits it. Generally, if a strategy changes over time it is most appropriate to create a new composite; accordingly, the redefinition of an existing composite should be a highly unusual event.
rationales.B: Performance divergence is not one of the two permitted grounds. Reassignment requires either a documented client revision of the mandate, objective, or strategy, or a redefinition of the composite. Moving a portfolio because its returns drifted from the composite average would let a firm reshape reported composite results at will, which is precisely what the switching restriction is designed to prevent.
rationales.C: No verifier-approval condition exists. What the standards require is documentation of the qualifying change itself, either the revised client mandate, objective, or strategy or the redefinition of the composite, rather than the prior written consent of an independent verifier. Verification addresses a firm's policies and procedures, not individual composite assignments.

questions.stem: A significant cash flow is most likely:

options.A: a client-directed flow large enough to disrupt strategy implementation.
options.B: any external flow above a GIPS-prescribed share of composite assets.
options.C: a firm-initiated transfer between portfolios in one composite.

rationales.A: A significant cash flow is a client-directed cash flow sufficiently large that it may temporarily prevent the firm from implementing the strategy. Significant cash flows are more likely to be an issue for strategies such as fixed income and emerging markets, where the liquidity of the underlying securities inhibits the ability to quickly invest incoming cash or to conduct an orderly sale of portfolio securities to meet a cash outflow. Firms must define significance on an ex ante, composite-specific basis and must consistently follow that composite-specific significant cash flow policy. In the event of a significant cash flow, a portfolio may be temporarily removed from the composite; alternatively, firms may use temporary new accounts to remove the effect of the flow.
rationales.B: No fixed percentage is prescribed by the GIPS standards. Each firm defines significance itself, ex ante and composite by composite, and must then apply that policy consistently, so there is no single threshold that applies across firms or across a firm's composites.
rationales.C: The concept concerns client-directed external flows large enough to disrupt implementation of the strategy. A firm-initiated rebalancing transfer among portfolios in the same composite is not client-directed and is not what triggers temporary removal from a composite or the use of a temporary new account.

questions.stem: Minimum asset levels for inclusion in a composite are most likely:

options.A: set at each firm's discretion.
options.B: prohibited.
options.C: fixed at a uniform level by the GIPS standards.

rationales.A: A firm may set a minimum asset level above which portfolios are eligible for inclusion in a composite; portfolios below that level are considered non-discretionary with respect to that composite. If a firm establishes a minimum, it must document policies addressing how portfolios are treated if they fall below it. A firm may elect to remove portfolios the month after they fall below the minimum, or it may determine that the minimum required to add a portfolio is $1 million while a portfolio is not removed unless its assets fall below $900,000. Any changes to a composite-specific minimum asset level must not be applied retroactively. If a portfolio is removed because it fell below the minimum, its prior performance must remain in the composite, and the firm must determine whether the removed portfolio meets any other composite definition and include it there in a timely and consistent manner.
rationales.B: Firms are expressly allowed to establish a composite-specific minimum asset level, below which portfolios are treated as non-discretionary for that composite. Nothing in the standards obliges a firm to admit every portfolio irrespective of size; what the standards require is that the minimum, if set, be documented and applied consistently.
rationales.C: No minimum is prescribed by the GIPS standards. A firm may set and document its own composite-specific minimum asset level, and figures such as a $1 million threshold for admission with a $900,000 floor for removal are illustrations of levels a firm might choose, not required amounts. Any change to the level must not be applied retroactively.

questions.stem: Sample policy language on switching portfolios between composites most likely:

options.A: allows moves at the manager's discretion.
options.B: allows moves only on redefinition or documented client changes.
options.C: is discouraged by the standards.

rationales.A: Manager judgment that another composite is a better fit is not a basis for a move. The sample policy language conditions a switch on a redefinition of the composite or on documented changes in the client's guidelines that require restructuring the portfolio, and the historical performance stays with the original composite either way.
rationales.B: A sample statement for such a policy reads: 'Portfolios shall not be moved from one composite to another unless the composite is redefined or documented changes in the client's guidelines require restructuring the portfolio in such a way that another composite becomes more appropriate. The portfolio shall be removed from the original composite at the end of the last calendar month before the event causing the removal occurred and shall be added to the appropriate new composite at the beginning of the calendar month following the date on which the portfolio is substantially invested. The historical performance of the portfolio shall remain in the original composite.'
rationales.C: Written policy language is exactly what the standards contemplate, which is why a sample statement of this kind exists. Firms are expected to document a switching policy, including the timing of removal and re-addition and the treatment of historical performance, and then apply it consistently rather than treat each move as a one-off judgment.

drills.los_text: explain requirements of the GIPS standards with respect to presentation and reporting
drills.reading_name: Overview of the Global Investment Performance Standards

questions.stem: A type of GIPS Report that a compliant firm must provide to prospective clients is most likely the GIPS:

options.A: Gross-of-Fees Report.
options.B: Composite Report.
options.C: Firm Report.

rationales.A: Gross-of-fees and net-of-fees results are presentation choices made within a report, not separate types of report. The two types are the GIPS Composite Report and the GIPS Pooled Fund Report.
rationales.B: Firms claiming compliance with the GIPS standards must make every reasonable effort to provide a GIPS Report to all prospective clients and limited distribution pooled fund investors, and the report provided must be the one that represents the strategy being marketed to the prospect. There are two types of GIPS Report. A GIPS Composite Report includes all of the information required by the GIPS standards for a specific composite; a GIPS Pooled Fund Report includes all of the information required by the GIPS standards for a specific pooled fund.
rationales.C: There is no firm-wide GIPS Report. The two report types each cover a single vehicle, a specific composite or a specific pooled fund, so a single report spanning all of a firm's strategies at once is not one of them.

questions.stem: For a GIPS Composite Report that includes time-weighted returns, the annual performance a firm must present is most likely:

options.A: 1 year, with no later extension.
options.B: 5 years, extended annually to 10.
options.C: 10 years from the first report.

rationales.A: One year is not the floor, and the record cannot be left where it starts. Five years of annual performance is the minimum, or returns since inception if the composite has existed for less than five years, and the compliant record must then be extended each year.
rationales.B: For each GIPS Composite Report that includes time-weighted returns, the GIPS standards require that firms show at least 5 years of annual performance, unless the composite has been in existence for less than 5 years, and that the GIPS-compliant performance record must then be extended each year until at least 10 years of performance have been presented. If the composite has been in existence for less than 5 years, the firm may present returns since inception and build over time to the 10 years of required returns.
rationales.C: The initial minimum is 5 years, or since inception where the composite is younger than that, building to 10 years one year at a time. A new composite can therefore produce a compliant report well before a decade of history exists.

questions.stem: A required element of a GIPS Composite Report presenting time-weighted returns is most likely:

options.A: the number of portfolios in every composite.
options.B: three-year annualized tracking error.
options.C: annual composite and benchmark returns.

rationales.A: The number of portfolios must be presented only when the composite contains six or more at the period end, so it is not required for every composite. The elements required of every such report are the annual composite and benchmark returns, the amount of assets in the composite, and total firm assets at the end of each period, together with the dispersion and standard deviation measures where their conditions are met.
rationales.B: The required risk measure is the three-year annualized ex post standard deviation of the composite and benchmark returns, presented as of each annual period end where monthly composite returns are available. Tracking error of the composite against its benchmark is not among the required elements.
rationales.C: The core elements of a GIPS Composite Report that presents a time-weighted return include composite and benchmark annual returns for all years; the number of portfolios, if six or more, in the composite at each period end; the amount of assets in the composite; the amount of total firm assets at the end of each period; a measure of internal dispersion of individual portfolio returns for each annual period if the composite contains six or more portfolios for the full year; and, if monthly composite returns are available, a three-year annualized ex post standard deviation of the composite and benchmark returns as of each annual period end.

questions.stem: A measure of internal dispersion most likely:

options.A: must be presented for each annual period.
options.B: is recommended rather than required.
options.C: measures variation relative to the benchmark.

rationales.A: The GIPS standards require that for each annual period a measure of internal dispersion of the returns earned by individual portfolios in the composite be presented. The requirement is intended to allow users to see how consistently the firm implemented its strategy across individual portfolios. A wide range of results should prompt the recipient to inquire about possible causes of the variability of returns to portfolios purportedly managed in accordance with the same strategy, and may suggest, among other possibilities, that the composite is defined too broadly. Only portfolios in the composite for the entire year are included in the calculation. The standards do not limit firms to a single measure of internal dispersion; the method chosen should fairly represent the range of returns for each annual period.
rationales.B: An annual internal dispersion measure is required, not merely recommended, subject only to limited exceptions for very small composites, such as those with five or fewer portfolios for the full year. A firm may choose among measures, but it may not choose whether to present one.
rationales.C: Internal dispersion measures the spread of individual portfolio returns within the composite, which is what shows how consistently the strategy was implemented across accounts. Benchmark-relative risk is a different matter and is captured, where required, by the three-year annualized ex post standard deviation of composite and benchmark returns.

questions.stem: Under the 2020 GIPS Standards for Firms, the three-year annualized ex post standard deviation is most likely required for:

options.A: the composite only.
options.B: both the composite and the benchmark.
options.C: neither the composite nor the benchmark.

rationales.A: The variability information required covers both the composite and the benchmark. Presenting the composite figure alone would defeat the purpose of the requirement, since the prospective client could not see the strategy's variability against the variability of the market it is measured against.
rationales.B: The 2020 GIPS Standards for Firms require that firms present information about the historical variability of composite and benchmark returns. Specifically, where monthly composite returns are available, firms must present, as of each annual period end, the three-year annualized ex post standard deviation of the monthly returns of both the composite and the benchmark. The rationale is to give prospective clients an indication of the risk of an investment strategy as executed by the firms under consideration. Because all GIPS Composite Reports include the same risk measure, and that measure is based on historical experience rather than subjective inputs, the GIPS standards allow for some degree of comparability among firms that claim compliance.
rationales.C: The 2020 standards retain the historical-variability presentation requirement rather than removing it. Where monthly composite returns are available, the three-year annualized ex post standard deviation must be presented as of each annual period end, and its uniformity across reports is what makes limited comparison between compliant firms possible.

questions.stem: The wording of a firm's GIPS compliance statement is most likely:

options.A: prescribed by the GIPS standards.
options.B: reviewed by CFA Institute before publication.
options.C: chosen freely by the firm.

rationales.A: The GIPS standards prescribe the language of the compliance statement; the firm supplies only its own name and, if applicable, its verification dates. The required wording for a firm that has been verified reads: 'Spinning Top Investments claims compliance with the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS®) and has prepared and presented this report in compliance with the GIPS standards. Spinning Top Investments has been independently verified for the periods 1 January 2011 to 31 December 2020. The verification report is available upon request. A firm that claims compliance with the GIPS standards must establish policies and procedures for complying with all the applicable requirements of the GIPS standards. Verification provides assurance on whether the firm's policies and procedures related to composite and pooled fund maintenance, as well as the calculation, presentation, and distribution of performance, have been designed in compliance with the GIPS standards and have been implemented on a firm-wide basis. Verification does not provide assurance on the accuracy of any specific performance report.' Note what the prescribed language does and does not promise: the firm must establish policies and procedures for complying with all applicable requirements, and verification speaks to the design and firm-wide implementation of those policies and procedures, not to the accuracy of any specific performance report. A firm that has not been verified uses the separate prescribed wording for an unverified claim.
rationales.B: CFA Institute does not pre-review or approve firm reports, and no such approval is available. Responsibility for claiming compliance correctly, and for using the prescribed compliance statement correctly, rests entirely with the firm. Independent assurance, where a firm wants it, comes from verification by an independent third party, which is recommended rather than required, not from any review by CFA Institute.
rationales.C: Compliance statements are not free-form. Prescribed language exists, with one version for a firm that has been verified and another for a firm that has not, and the firm inserts its name and verification periods into that wording rather than drafting its own. Fixing the language is what makes the claim comparable across firms and keeps a firm from overstating what its compliance claim or its verification actually covers.

questions.stem: When a firm uses a model fee to compute net-of-fees composite returns, the fee it deducts is most likely:

options.A: a model fee based on the highest applicable fee schedule.
options.B: each client's actual negotiated fee.
options.C: a model fee based on the lowest applicable fee schedule.

rationales.A: Net-of-fees returns may be calculated by deducting a model management fee from the monthly gross composite return, and the conservative model input is the highest fee applicable to the composite: with a highest management fee of 1.00% per year, the monthly deduction is 1.00%/12 = 0.083% of the gross composite return. This sits alongside the related return conventions: gross-of-fees returns are presented before management and custodial fees but after all trading expenses, and composite and benchmark returns are presented gross of non-reclaimable withholding taxes. Using the highest applicable fee means the reported net return cannot flatter any client who pays that schedule or less.
rationales.B: A model fee is permitted; a firm is not obliged to compute net-of-fees composite returns from each client's actual negotiated fee. Where a model fee is used, the method deducts 1/12th of the highest applicable annual management fee from each month's gross composite return — 0.083% monthly on a 1.00% annual fee — and the firm discloses that a model fee was used.
rationales.C: The lowest fee schedule is the wrong model input, because deducting the smallest fee any client pays would overstate net performance for everyone else. The highest applicable fee is used precisely because it is conservative: 1.00% per year deducted as 0.083% per month from the gross composite return.

questions.stem: A composite description in a GIPS Composite Report is most likely required to include:

options.A: the strategy, key material risks, the account minimum and its history, and any prior name.
options.B: a standardized description template identical across all compliant firms.
options.C: only the composite's name and its benchmark.

rationales.A: A composite description must convey the strategy or mandate, the key material risks, the account minimum and any historical changes to it, and any prior name of the composite. An illustrative description reads: 'The Large Cap Growth Composite includes all institutional portfolios that invest in large-cap US stocks that are considered to have growth in earnings prospects that are superior to that of the average company within the XYZ Large Cap Growth Index. Key material risks include the risks that stock prices will decline and that the composite will underperform its benchmark. The account minimum for the composite is $5 million. Prior to July 2016, the account minimum was $2 million. Prior to March 2020, the name of the composite was the Growth Composite.' Each element has a purpose: the strategy lets a prospective client judge comparability, the risks warn what the return series can do, the account minimum and its history explain which portfolios are and were eligible for inclusion, and the prior name lets a reader tie the record to performance they may have seen presented under the old label.
rationales.B: The GIPS standards prescribe required content, not a standardized template. Each firm writes its own description in its own words, and that description must cover the strategy or mandate, the key material risks, the account minimum and any historical changes to it, and any prior composite name. Strategies differ too much for one form of words to serve them all; what is standardized is the list of things that must be conveyed.
rationales.C: Name and benchmark are not enough. The description must also convey the strategy or mandate and the key material risks, and it must disclose the account minimum together with any historical changes to it, as well as any prior name of the composite. None of that content is merely recommended.

drills.los_text: explain the conditions under which the performance of a past firm or affiliation may be linked to or used to represent the historical performance of a new or acquiring firm
drills.reading_name: Overview of the Global Investment Performance Standards

questions.stem: Under the GIPS standards, performance earned at a prior firm is most likely:

options.A: retained by the managers who earned it as a personal record.
options.B: barred from linkage to the new firm's record.
options.C: linked to the new firm's record if specified conditions are met.

rationales.A: Performance belongs to the firm, not to the individuals who produced it, so it does not travel with a manager as a personal track record. Performance from a past firm or affiliation may be linked to the performance of the new or acquiring firm only where that firm meets the portability requirements, which are applied on a composite-specific basis: substantially all the investment decision makers are employed by the new or acquiring firm; the decision-making process remains substantially intact and independent within the new or acquiring firm; the new or acquiring firm has records that document and support the reported performance; and there is no break in the track record between the past firm or affiliation and the new or acquiring firm.
rationales.B: Portability is permitted, conditionally, rather than prohibited; a firm does not have to restart its record at its own inception. The portability of past performance is a complex and sometimes contentious subject, but the standards resolve it with four tests rather than a ban, and a firm that meets them for a given composite may link the prior record.
rationales.C: Performance from a past firm or affiliation may be linked to the performance of the new or acquiring firm if the new or acquiring firm meets certain requirements. The requirements, which apply on a composite-specific basis, are that (1) substantially all the investment decision makers are employed by the new or acquiring firm, (2) the decision-making process remains substantially intact and independent within the new or acquiring firm, (3) the new or acquiring firm has records that document and support the reported performance, and (4) there is no break in the track record between the past firm or affiliation and the new or acquiring firm. Read together, the four tests ask whether the same people, running the same process, produced a documented and uninterrupted record — that is, whether the prior performance is genuinely the new firm's own.

questions.stem: If there is a break in the track record between the past firm and the acquiring firm, the prior performance is most likely:

options.A: presented, but not linked to the new record.
options.B: linked by interpolating returns across the gap.
options.C: unusable in any form.

rationales.A: Where there is a break in the track record between the past firm and the new or acquiring firm, and the first three portability tests are met — substantially all the investment decision makers are employed by the new or acquiring firm, the decision-making process remains substantially intact and independent within it, and it has records that document and support the reported performance — the performance from the past firm or affiliation may be used to represent the historical performance of the new or acquiring firm, but the two performance records may not be linked. The distinction matters: the prior record may be shown, so the reader sees the history, yet it may not be chained to the new record into a single continuous return series, because the gap means no one managed the strategy across it.
rationales.B: Interpolation is never an answer to a break. The returns across the gap were not earned, so estimating them would manufacture a continuous series out of a period in which the strategy was not being run. The records stand unlinked on either side of the break, and the fourth portability test — no break in the track record — is precisely what fails here.
rationales.C: A break limits how the prior performance may be presented; it does not bar its use. With the first three portability tests met, the performance from the past firm or affiliation may still be used to represent the historical performance of the new or acquiring firm. What the break costs is linkage: the two records may not be joined into one continuous series.

questions.stem: When a GIPS-compliant firm acquires another firm, the acquired non-compliant assets are most likely:

options.A: required to comply before the acquisition closes.
options.B: permanently exempt as legacy business.
options.C: allowed a one-year grace period to comply.

rationales.A: Compliance is not demanded at closing. The standards recognize that an acquirer cannot retrofit another firm's records and processes instantly, so a GIPS-compliant firm that acquires another firm or affiliation is given a one-year grace period after the acquisition to bring any non-compliant assets into compliance for future reporting periods.
rationales.B: The relief is temporary, not permanent. Treating acquired assets as legacy business exempt indefinitely would let a compliant firm hold a growing pool of non-compliant assets while still claiming firm-wide compliance, which is exactly what the one-year limit prevents: once the grace period ends, the acquired assets must comply for future reporting periods.
rationales.C: If a GIPS-compliant firm acquires another firm or affiliation, the firm is given a one-year grace period to bring any non-compliant assets into compliance for future reporting periods. The grace period runs from the acquisition and is forward-looking — it buys time to align policies, procedures, composite construction and records, not a permanent exemption, and it does not retroactively make the acquired history compliant.

questions.stem: Performance earned at a prior affiliation and linked by the acquiring firm is most likely:

options.A: presented without any accompanying disclosure.
options.B: transferred automatically with the investment team.
options.C: disclosed as having been earned at the prior affiliation.

rationales.A: Linked prior performance must be identified as such, which is why prescribed disclosure language exists for it. A reader who is shown a continuous record is entitled to know that part of it was earned elsewhere, by whom, and on what basis it was linked; without that disclosure the presentation would imply the whole record was produced at the presenting firm.
rationales.B: Nothing transfers automatically when a team changes firms. Linkage rests on the portability conditions being met on a composite-specific basis: substantially all the investment decision makers are employed by the new or acquiring firm, the decision-making process remains substantially intact and independent within it, that firm has records that document and support the reported performance, and there is no break in the track record.
rationales.C: The disclosure accompanying linked prior performance states where it was earned and why linkage is proper: 'Performance prior to May 2014 occurred while the investment management team was affiliated with another firm. The investment management team has managed the composite since its inception, and the investment process has not changed. The historical performance has been linked to performance earned at Spinning Top Investments.' A companion note explains the transaction and the limits of what is shown: 'Spinning Top Investments acquired the composite through an acquisition of ABC Capital in May 2014. Firm assets prior to 2014 are not presented because the composite was not part of the firm.' Each clause maps onto a portability test — the same team (decision makers employed by the new firm), an unchanged process (substantially intact and independent), and continuity since inception (no break) — and the firm-assets note shows that porting a composite's record does not port firm-level assets for periods before the composite belonged to the firm.

questions.stem: The GIPS portability requirements are most likely applied on:

options.A: a firm-wide basis.
options.B: an individual manager basis.
options.C: a composite-specific basis.

rationales.A: The tests are not applied once for the whole firm. Each composite must independently satisfy all four requirements, so meeting them for one composite ports that composite's record and nothing else. An acquisition may well carry some strategies across intact while others lose their decision makers, change their process, or arrive without supporting records.
rationales.B: Performance belongs to the firm rather than to an individual, so the requirements are not assessed manager by manager and a record does not follow a person as a personal track record. Portability is assessed composite by composite, and one of the tests is whether substantially all the investment decision makers for that composite are employed by the new or acquiring firm.
rationales.C: The portability requirements apply on a composite-specific basis, not firm-wide. Performance can be ported for the specific composites where all the requirements are met, and it is not automatically applied across the firm. Each composite is evaluated independently against whether (1) substantially all the investment decision makers are employed by the new or acquiring firm, (2) the decision-making process remains substantially intact and independent within that firm, (3) the new or acquiring firm has records that document and support the reported performance, and (4) there is no break in the track record between the past firm or affiliation and the new or acquiring firm.

questions.stem: Portability of a composite's track record to an acquiring firm most likely requires:

options.A: a decision-making process that remains substantially intact and independent.
options.B: a decision-making process replaced by the acquiring firm's own.
options.C: no condition on the process beyond retaining its decision makers.

rationales.A: The requirement is that the decision-making process remain substantially intact and independent within the new or acquiring firm, and both modifiers do work. Substantially intact is continuity: the process that produced the prior returns is still the process being run. Independent is autonomy: it still operates on its own within the acquirer. If the process is subsumed into a different process at the new firm, or stops operating independently, portability may fail even though the record and the people came across. Paired with the requirement that substantially all the investment decision makers are employed by the new or acquiring firm, the pair asks whether the same key people are still making decisions in essentially the same way.
rationales.B: Replacing the process with the acquirer's own established process defeats the continuity the test demands. What the standards require is that the decision-making process remain substantially intact and independent within the new or acquiring firm; a record produced by one process cannot be presented as the history of a strategy now run by a different one.
rationales.C: Retaining the people is one test, not the whole of it. Substantially all the investment decision makers must be employed by the new or acquiring firm and, separately, the decision-making process must remain substantially intact and independent within that firm. Keeping the decision makers while folding their process into the acquirer's own would satisfy the first condition and fail the second.

drills.los_text: discuss the purpose, scope, and process of verification
drills.reading_name: Overview of the Global Investment Performance Standards

questions.stem: Verification under the GIPS standards is best described as:

options.A: a certification of each composite's reported returns.
options.B: an assessment of the firm's policies and procedures.
options.C: a mandatory annual audit of the firm.

rationales.A: Verification does not certify returns. It assesses, firm-wide, the policies and procedures for constructing composites and for calculating and presenting performance in light of the requirements of the GIPS standards, and it expressly does not provide assurance as to the accuracy of any particular composite or pooled fund presentation. A firm wanting assurance on a specific presentation needs a performance examination of that composite or pooled fund, which is a separate engagement.
rationales.B: Verification may be characterized as a process in which an independent expert assesses a firm's policies and procedures for constructing composites and calculating and presenting performance in light of the requirements of the GIPS standards. Its purpose is to give the firm and the users of its GIPS Reports greater confidence in the firm's claim of compliance. Two limits define its scope: it is performed on a firm-wide basis, so it cannot be carried out on a single composite, and it does not provide assurance as to the accuracy of any particular composite or pooled fund presentation. The GIPS standards recommend that firms undergo verification.
rationales.C: Verification is voluntary, though recommended; it is not a condition of claiming compliance. A firm may claim compliance without having been verified, and it discloses whether or not it has been verified, with the prescribed compliance statement differing between the two cases.

questions.stem: GIPS verification is most likely:

options.A: conducted by an independent third party.
options.B: conducted by the firm's internal compliance department.
options.C: conducted on a single composite selected by the firm.

rationales.A: Verification must be performed by a qualified and independent third party. It provides assurance on whether the firm's policies and procedures related to composite and pooled fund maintenance, as well as the calculation, presentation, and distribution of performance, have been designed in compliance with the GIPS standards and have been implemented on a firm-wide basis. The verifier must conduct the verification in accordance with the GIPS Standards for Verifiers. A single verification report is issued only with respect to the whole firm, so verification cannot be carried out on a single composite or pooled fund. A firm that does not meet all the requirements of the GIPS standards may not state or in any other way represent that it is in compliance; it cannot claim that one composite is 'in compliance' or that all of its equity strategies are 'in compliance.'
rationales.B: Verification must be performed by a qualified, independent third party. The firm's own compliance or performance-measurement department is part of the firm and therefore is not independent, so work it performs cannot constitute verification under the GIPS standards, however rigorous that internal work may be. Internal review of policies and procedures is useful preparation for verification, but it is not a substitute for it.
rationales.C: A single verification report is issued only with respect to the whole firm. Verification is a firm-wide engagement and cannot be carried out on a single composite or pooled fund selected by the firm, and a firm may not claim that one composite is in compliance while the rest of the firm is not. A detailed review of one or more specific composites or pooled funds is a performance examination, which is a separate engagement available only in addition to firm-wide verification.

questions.stem: A performance examination under the GIPS standards is most likely:

options.A: another name for the firm-wide verification engagement.
options.B: mandatory each year for the firm's five largest composites.
options.C: optional and conducted on specific composites or pooled funds.

rationales.A: A performance examination is not a renamed verification. It is a distinct, detailed engagement conducted on one or more specific composites or pooled funds, and it is available only in addition to verification. Verification is firm-wide and assesses whether the firm's policies and procedures have been designed in compliance with the GIPS standards and implemented on a firm-wide basis; an examination goes further, on a narrower subject. Issuing the verifier's report does not convert verification into an examination.
rationales.B: Performance examinations are optional and firm-selected. Nothing in the GIPS standards makes them mandatory, annual, or keyed to composite size, so a requirement covering a compliant firm's five largest composites measured by year-end composite assets does not exist. A verified firm chooses whether to have an examination and chooses which composites or pooled funds it covers.
rationales.C: A firm that is verified may choose to have a detailed performance examination conducted on one or more specific composites or pooled funds, and it may state that a composite has been examined if a performance examination report has been issued for that specific composite. A performance examination is separate from verification: verification is firm-wide and is the prerequisite, while an examination applies to the specific composite or composites, or pooled fund or funds, the firm selects.

questions.stem: In a GIPS verification engagement, the verifier is most likely required to:

options.A: rely on management's representations about the firm.
options.B: limit the work to recalculating a sample of composite returns.
options.C: understand the firm's structure, operations, policies, and procedures.

rationales.A: Bare reliance on management's representations is not sufficient; independent understanding and testing define the engagement. Verifiers must learn about the firm, including its corporate structure and how it operates, and they must not only obtain a copy of the firm's GIPS-related policies and procedures but also ensure that all applicable policies and procedures are properly included and adequately documented.
rationales.B: Recalculating returns is only part of the engagement. Verifiers must understand the firm, including its corporate structure and how it operates, its policies and procedures for complying with all applicable requirements and adopted recommendations of the GIPS standards, and the policies, procedures, and methodologies it uses to value portfolios and compute investment performance. That understanding extends well beyond recalculation of a sample of composite returns.
rationales.C: Verifiers must learn about the firm, including its corporate structure and how it operates, and they must understand the firm's policies and procedures for complying with all applicable requirements and adopted recommendations of the GIPS standards. Verifiers must not only obtain a copy of the firm's GIPS-related policies and procedures but also ensure that all applicable policies and procedures are properly included and adequately documented. Finally, verifiers must understand the policies, procedures, and methodologies the firm uses to value portfolios and compute investment performance.

questions.stem: In a GIPS verification, the verifier's required testing most likely:

options.A: may be performed on a sample of portfolios.
options.B: must cover every portfolio and composite at the firm.
options.C: may not be performed on a sample of portfolios.

rationales.A: Although verification is conducted on a firm-wide basis, verifiers may use a sampling methodology to conduct the required testing. When selecting sample portfolios, verifiers must take into consideration the number of composites and pooled funds at the firm and the number of portfolios in each composite. They must also take into account total assets under management, the internal control structure at the firm, the number of years being verified, the systems used in the construction and maintenance of composites, the method of calculating performance, and whether the firm uses external performance measurement services. The selection of sample accounts for testing is a critical step in the verification process: if the verifier encounters errors or discovers that the firm's record-keeping is deficient, a larger sample or additional verification procedures may be warranted.
rationales.B: Verification is firm-wide in scope, but firm-wide scope does not require testing every portfolio and composite without exception. Verifiers may use a sampling methodology to conduct the required testing, sizing and selecting the sample by reference to the number of composites and pooled funds, the number of portfolios in each composite, total assets under management, the internal control structure, the number of years being verified, the systems used to construct and maintain composites, the method of calculating performance, and whether external performance measurement services are used.
rationales.C: Sampling methodologies are expressly permitted in verification. Rather than prohibiting sampling because some accounts would go untested, the standards manage that risk through how the sample is chosen and sized, and they require escalation when problems appear: if the verifier encounters errors or discovers that record-keeping is deficient, a larger sample or additional verification procedures may be warranted.

questions.stem: The benefits to a firm of undergoing GIPS verification most likely include:

options.A: satisfaction of securities-regulatory requirements only.
options.B: marketing language for pitch books and nothing more.
options.C: a more credible compliance claim and improved internal processes.

rationales.A: Verification is voluntary and is not a securities-regulatory requirement, so satisfying regulation is not the benefit it delivers. Its benefits are that it makes the claim of compliance on a firm-wide basis more credible and that it improves the firm itself: increased knowledge in the performance measurement team, consistently higher quality of performance presentations, improved internal processes and procedures, and potential marketing advantages.
rationales.B: Potential marketing advantage is one benefit among several, not the whole of it. Verification makes the claim of compliance on a firm-wide basis more credible and also delivers substantive internal benefits: increased knowledge in the performance measurement team, consistently higher quality of performance presentations, and improved internal processes and procedures. Above all, it supports the guiding principles of fair representation and full disclosure of investment performance, which is more than pitch-book language.
rationales.C: In addition to making the claim of compliance on a firm-wide basis more credible, the verification process may benefit the firm in other ways: increased knowledge in the performance measurement team, consistently higher quality of performance presentations, improved internal processes and procedures, and potential marketing advantages. Above all, verification supports the guiding principles of fair representation and full disclosure of investment performance.
